claims.text: Isolated chemical short-range-order clusters initially reduce thermal conductivity by increasing phonon scattering.
Above a critical connectivity threshold, percolating SRO clusters increase thermal conductivity by forming coherent, low-scattering pathways.
The resulting thermal-conductivity response to increasing SRO is non-monotonic.
A random-solid-solution HfNbTaTiZr or MoNbTaW alloy has low thermal conductivity because mass variance and lattice distortion strongly scatter phonons.
Controlled annealing or rapid quenching can evolve SRO from a random state through isolated clusters to a percolating network.
The proposed 300–1000 K regime remains below the order-disorder transition temperature and retains a stable single bcc phase.
Percolating SRO forms a connected network associated with diffuse antiphase boundaries.
The connected SRO network constitutes a distinct phonon-transport channel, unlike isolated SRO clusters.
Local chemical order reduces effective mass-variance and lattice-distortion scattering along the percolating network.
The SRO network can short-circuit the dominant random-alloy scattering events.
In MoNbTaW, SRO flattens the energy landscape and reduces solute drag for edge-dislocation motion.
The dislocation-energy-landscape effect in MoNbTaW is analogous to a reduction of phonon scattering by percolating SRO.
Thermal conductivity reaches a minimum in the isolated-cluster regime and then rises significantly upon SRO percolation.
A sufficiently coherent percolating SRO network can produce conductivity exceeding that of the random solid solution.
Serial and parallel effective-medium mixing models cannot predict the magnitude of the proposed nonlinear conductivity increase.
Heating above the order-disorder transition temperature causes SRO to disappear as the alloy homogenizes.
Formation of long-range intermetallic phases or precipitates would invalidate the proposed SRO-percolation mechanism by changing the electronic structure and scattering behavior.
The critical SRO percolation threshold in bcc refractory high-entropy alloys is unknown.
Quantifying the proposed effect requires an atomistic potential that correctly captures the SRO potential-energy landscape and its evolution.

A controlled series combining SRO measurements, cluster-connectivity measurements, and TDTR conductivity measurements can test whether conductivity enhancement coincides with percolation rather than merely with increasing SRO.
